unitObjectives.objective: Pupils will be able to describe how global warming affects Arctic ice and animals using cause-and-effect language ('because' and 'so').
Pupils will be able to read and interpret stanzas of a narrative poem ('The Bear and I') identifying sensory imagery and rhyme.
Pupils will be able to compare traditional gasoline cars with green vehicle alternatives (electric, solar, biofuel) using comparative adjectives ('cleaner', 'quieter', 'more expensive').
Pupils will be able to pronounce and spell words with the final consonant blend '-ng' (/ŋ/ sound: sing, long, reading, bang, spring).
Pupils will be able to use 'instead of' to express eco-friendly choices ('clean cars use electricity instead of gasoline').
Pupils will be able to write a 4-sentence comparison or environmental action plan to protect wildlife.

canDo.statement: I can explain why the Arctic sea ice is melting.
I can read aloud lines from the poem 'The Bear and I'.
I can compare an electric car and a gasoline car.
I can read and spell words ending with '-ng' like sing, spring, and long.
I can explain how clean cars help protect polar bears.
I can use 'because' and 'so' to explain environmental causes and results.

reading.objective: Analyze poetry elements (stanzas, imagery, rhythm) and compare informational science texts using feature charts.

listening.objective: Listen to scientific explanations of renewable energy and identify vehicle attributes from audio cues.

speaking.objective: Participate in choral poetry recitations and debate the advantages and drawbacks of different car types.

writing.objective: Complete a comparison matrix and write a short paragraph contrasting two types of vehicles.

vocabulary.objective: Acquire and use 12 target words and terms related to climate, Arctic biomes, and vehicle engineering.

grammar.objective: Form comparative adjectives (short root + -er vs more + long root) and connect clauses with 'because', 'so', and 'instead of'.

phonics.objective: Articulate the voiced velar nasal /ŋ/ at the end of syllables without adding a hard /g/ or /k/ stop.

content.objective: Understand the relationship between fossil fuel combustion, greenhouse warming, and polar habitat loss.

thinking.objective: Differentiate between fact and opinion, and map complex multi-step environmental cause-and-effect chains.

values.objective: Develop environmental stewardship, empathy for vulnerable animals, and respect for sustainable engineering.

successCriteria.criterion: Pupil accurately states: 'Electric cars are quieter than gasoline cars.'
Pupil recites the poem line 'We are not enemies today' with proper rhythm and expression.
Pupil completes the Car Features Matrix on page 54 with 100% accurate classification.
Pupil clearly articulates the difference between 'thin' and 'thing' in phonics practice.

The bear and man are not enemies.
They stopped and were not enemies.

chunks.meaning: In place of someone or something; as an alternative.
chunks.bookExample: Clean cars use electricity instead of gasoline. (p.51)
easyExamples: Drink water instead of soda.
Walk instead of driving.
Use solar power instead of oil.

chunks.chunk: made a trap for us both
chunks.meaning: Created a dangerous situation where neither person can easily get out.
chunks.bookExample: The warm sun has made a trap for us both. (p.44)
easyExamples: The ice made a trap for us.
Melting snow made a trap.
The mud was a trap for cars.

chunks.meaning: Taking care of the earth and stopping pollution.
chunks.bookExample: Clean cars help protect our planet. (p.53)
easyExamples: We must protect our planet.
Clean energy protects our planet.
Save water to protect our planet.

chunks.meaning: Stating an opinion and giving a logical reason.
chunks.bookExample: I think electric cars are better because they make no smoke.
easyExamples: I think solar cars are good because they use the sun.
I think ice is thin because it is warm.
I think we should walk because it is clean.

chunks.meaning: Asking about cause-and-effect outcomes in science.
chunks.bookExample: What happens when Arctic ice melts? (p.41)
easyExamples: What happens when ice warms up?
What happens when cars burn oil?
What happens when the sun shines?

chunks.meaning: Stating a result or solution clearly to the class.
easyExamples: My answer is solar power.
My answer is the polar bear.
My answer is True.

grammar.meaning: Comparing two vehicles, animals, or states.
grammar.use: Use short adjective + -er for 1-syllable words (cleaner, quieter, thinner); use 'more' for 3-syllable words (more expensive).
bookExamples: Electric cars are cleaner and quieter than traditional cars. (p.47)
Solar cars are more expensive than gasoline cars. (p.48)
grammar.simpleRule: Add -er to short words like 'clean', but put 'more' before long words like 'expensive'.
practiceSentences: An electric car is quieter than a gas car.
The ice is thinner today than yesterday.
A new solar car is more expensive than an old car.

commonTurkishL1Errors.error: Electric cars are more quiet than gas cars.
commonTurkishL1Errors.correction: Electric cars are quieter than gas cars.
commonTurkishL1Errors.explanation: Turkish students apply 'daha' (more) uniformly to all adjectives, leading to 'more quiet' instead of 'quieter'.

grammar.use: Use 'because' to state the reason; use 'so' to state the result.
bookExamples: The ice cracked because it was warm. (p.44)
Electric cars have batteries, so they make no smoke. (p.51)
grammar.simpleRule: 'Because' tells why it happened; 'so' tells what happened next.
practiceSentences: The bear ran because the ice cracked.
Gasoline cars make smoke, so the air gets dirty.
Solar cars use the sun, so they need daylight.

commonTurkishL1Errors.error: Because it was warm, so the ice cracked.
commonTurkishL1Errors.correction: Because it was warm, the ice cracked. / It was warm, so the ice cracked.
commonTurkishL1Errors.explanation: Turkish learners often use both 'because' (çünkü) and 'so' (bu yüzden) in the same sentence.

grammar.form: Subject + Verb + Noun 1 + instead of + Noun 2
grammar.meaning: Expressing substitution of an eco-friendly option over a polluting one.
grammar.use: Use 'instead of' to show a positive alternative.
bookExamples: Biofuel cars use plants instead of oil. (p.50)
Clean cars use electricity instead of gasoline. (p.51)
grammar.simpleRule: Use 'instead of' when you choose the good thing and leave the bad thing behind.
practiceSentences: Ride a bike instead of taking a car.
Save energy instead of wasting it.

commonTurkishL1Errors.correction: Cars use electricity instead of gasoline.
commonTurkishL1Errors.explanation: Turkish learners frequently drop the preposition 'of'.

modelDialogue: A: Look at that red car and that white car! Which one do you like?
B: I like the white electric car.
B: Yes! It is much quieter than the red car, and it makes no dirty smoke.
A: Why is the Arctic sea ice melting?
B: Because the air is getting warmer from pollution.
A: What happens to the polar bears?
B: The ice is too thin, so they cannot easily hunt for fish.
A: How can we protect polar bears in the Arctic?
B: We can drive clean electric cars instead of gasoline cars.
A: That is a great idea! Clean cars keep our air fresh.
B: Yes, and they help protect our planet for the future.

tongueTwister.text: The king can sing a strong spring song while reading.

phonics.turkishSpeakerDifficulties: Turkish speakers naturally replace the English velar nasal /ŋ/ with either a flat alveolar /n/ or they pronounce an aggressive hard /g/ or /k/ at the end ('sing-guh' or 'sink'). Teach students to feel the back of their tongue touch the soft palate while vibrating vocal cords, with no final release burst.

readings.title: The Bear and I
readings.mainIdea: An Arctic fisherman and a hungry polar bear face shared danger when thin sea ice cracks beneath them.
readings.summary: An Arctic fisherman sits quietly on the ice by a fishing hole in the freezing cold. Suddenly, a giant white polar bear walks toward him across the frozen sea. Both hunters are hungry and looking for fish to survive the winter. However, unusually warm weather has made the ice thin and fragile. When the heavy bear steps closer, the ice cracks loudly, trapping both man and beast on a small drifting ice floe. Recognizing that they are both scared and trying to survive, the fisherman steps back gently. The bear catches a fish from the hole and plunges into the water, swimming peacefully away.
keySentences: I sit by the hole in the ice, waiting for fish in the freezing wind. (p.43)
The great white bear steps near; the ice is thin and begins to crack. (p.44)
We are not enemies today; the warm sun has made a trap for us both. (p.45)

characters.name: The Fisherman

characters.name: The Polar Bear
characters.trait: Mighty, hungry predator made vulnerable by melting ice

readings.setting: Frozen Arctic sea, near a circular ice fishing hole, under an unseasonably warm sun
sequence: 1. The fisherman waits quietly by an ice hole in the freezing Arctic wind.
2. A large hungry polar bear walks across the ice toward the hole.
3. The thin ice begins to crack under the bear's heavy weight.
4. Both hunters are trapped on the breaking ice floe.
5. The fisherman steps back gently, realizing they share the same danger.
6. The bear catches a fish and dives into the water to swim safely away.

problemSolution.problem: The sea ice is melting and thin, cracking under the heavy bear.
problemSolution.solution: The fisherman gives the bear space so both avoid a fight, and the bear swims away.

readings.moralOrMessage: When faced with shared natural danger, humans and animals can coexist peacefully.

readings.title: Clean Cars
readings.mainIdea: Clean cars that use biofuels, electricity, and solar power help protect the environment from pollution and global warming.
readings.summary: Most traditional cars use gasoline, which comes from crude oil pumped from deep underground. When gasoline burns in car engines, it produces loud noise and dirty exhaust smoke that pollutes the air and warms the earth. To stop pollution, scientists have invented clean cars. Biofuel cars run on fuel made from plants like corn and sugar. Electric cars use large rechargeable batteries and quiet electric motors, making zero exhaust smoke. Solar cars collect clean power directly from sunlight using roof panels. Although clean cars are currently expensive to buy, they keep our air fresh and help protect Arctic animals from melting ice.
keySentences: Traditional cars burn gasoline, which makes dirty exhaust smoke and pollutes the air. (p.49)
Electric cars do not use gasoline; they run on powerful batteries and make no smoke. (p.51)
Clean cars help protect our planet and keep the air fresh for everyone. (p.53)

characters.name: Scientists & Engineers
characters.trait: Inventing clean vehicles to protect the planet

readings.setting: Modern busy city highways, engineering laboratories, sunny open roads
sequence: 1. Traditional cars burn oil and gasoline, creating dirty exhaust smoke and engine noise.
2. Air pollution causes the earth to get warmer and melts polar ice.
3. Inventors make biofuel from corn and plants instead of oil.
4. Engineers build electric cars powered by rechargeable batteries that produce zero emissions.
5. Designers build solar-powered cars with roof panels that collect energy from the sun.
6. Using clean cars keeps city air fresh and helps protect animals from climate change.

problemSolution.problem: Traditional cars create noise and dirty exhaust smog that causes global warming.
problemSolution.solution: Engineers develop electric, solar, and biofuel cars that produce zero smoke.

readings.moralOrMessage: Smart technology and human choices can heal our planet and protect wildlife.

content.clilTopic: Science & Technology: Climate Change, Arctic Habitats, and Clean Green Vehicles

keyFactsTeacherSaysAloud.fact: Polar bears depend on thick sea ice to walk and hunt seals; when ice melts early, they cannot catch food.
Scientists put bright non-toxic dye into glacial rivers to track how fast melted ice water flows into the sea.
Gasoline comes from crude oil that formed millions of years ago from ancient plants and sea creatures.
Electric cars are so quiet that engineers sometimes add artificial sounds so pedestrians can hear them coming!
Solar cars can travel thousands of kilometers using only clean sunshine collected by roof panels.

misconceptions.misconception: Children think polar bears and penguins live together in the same place.
misconceptions.clarification: Polar bears live only in the Arctic (North Pole); penguins live in Antarctica (South Pole).

misconceptions.misconception: Children think electric cars have no engines at all.
misconceptions.clarification: Electric cars have electric motors powered by batteries instead of fuel combustion engines.

realLifeLinksTurkey.link: Turkey has developed its own domestic electric vehicle, TOGG, which runs on rechargeable batteries with zero exhaust smoke.
Southern cities like Antalya and Izmir use large solar panel arrays to generate clean electricity from bright sunshine.

teacherInstructions.command: Compare the red car and the white car.
teacherInstructions.tr: Kırmızı araba ile beyaz arabayı karşılaştırın.

teacherInstructions.command: Say the word and feel the '-ng' sound in your throat.
teacherInstructions.tr: Kelimeyi söyleyin ve boğazınızdaki '-ng' sesini hissedin.

praisePhrases.phrase: You are a true planet protector!

fromUnit1And2.note: Provides background for polar wildlife survival.
Builds directly into 'so' and 'because' for environmental chains.
Contrasts with the new final consonant blend -ng.

fromUnit1And2.item: Basic vehicle and animal vocabulary (car, bear, fish, water)
fromUnit1And2.note: Core lexicon needed to access the texts.

canDoChecks.check: Can read aloud 2 lines from 'The Bear and I' with clear pronunciation.
canDoChecks.method: Observe choral and individual poetry readings.

canDoChecks.check: Can explain why sea ice is melting in simple English.
Can compare two cars using 'cleaner than' or 'quieter than'.
canDoChecks.method: Observe pair speaking task on p.47.

canDoChecks.check: Can explain what fuel electric cars use.
Can pronounce words ending in '-ng' without a hard 'g' click.
canDoChecks.method: Listen during phonics word work p.47.

canDoChecks.check: Can correctly complete the Car Features Matrix on p.54.
Can identify why the fisherman and bear are 'not enemies today'.
Can form a sentence with 'instead of' (e.g., 'solar power instead of oil').
Can trace the 4-step chain from car exhaust to polar bear habitats.
Can state one way children can help protect the planet.
canDoChecks.method: Collect closing oral responses in Lesson 8.

oralCheck.question: Where is the fisherman sitting in the poem?
oralCheck.expectedAnswer: On the Arctic sea ice by a fishing hole.

oralCheck.question: Why does the ice begin to crack?
oralCheck.expectedAnswer: Because the ice is thin and the bear is very heavy.

oralCheck.question: Which car is quieter: a gasoline car or an electric car?
What do solar cars use to make energy?
oralCheck.expectedAnswer: They use light from the sun.

oralCheck.question: What sound does the word 'spring' end with?

speakingRubric.developing: Speaks with fragmented single words; omits 'than' in comparisons ('electric quiet'); requires Turkish prompts.
speakingRubric.proficient: Uses comparative adjectives accurately ('quieter than', 'cleaner than'); explains causes with 'because'.
speakingRubric.advanced: Expresses complex ideas fluently; connects clean energy choices to wildlife preservation using 'instead of' and 'so'.

writingRubric.developing: Writes incomplete phrases; leaves feature matrix cells empty; misspells target vocabulary.
writingRubric.proficient: Completes the Car Features Matrix correctly; writes 2-3 accurate comparison sentences using sentence frames.
writingRubric.advanced: Produces a cohesive 4-sentence comparison paragraph with correct comparative forms, capitalization, and punctuation.

supportWeaker.description: Color-code comparative endings: green for 1-syllable + er (clean-er), purple for more + long word (more expensive).
Have students touch their throat to feel vocal cord vibration during the '-ng' nasal sound.
Desk cards with labeled vehicle icons and fuel types for quick visual reference.

challengeStronger.description: Design a futuristic clean vehicle and present 3 reasons why it is better than gasoline cars.
Write a 4-line rhyming stanza continuing the fisherman's journey after the bear swims away.
Role-play a city mayor deciding whether to replace city buses with electric buses.

lessonSequence.title: The Pink River: Tracking Planet Changes
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to discuss climate change and explain why the river is pink.

stages.activity: Display the bright pink river photo on smartboard; ask wonder questions.
Explain scientist dye experiments; introduce Big Idea: 'How is our world changing?'
Temperature slider activity: observe what happens when Arctic ice melts.
Pairs complete sentence frame: 'The ice melts because the air is ___.'
State one animal that lives in the Arctic.

lessonSequence.title: The Ice Hole: Waiting in the Freezing Wind
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to read stanzas 1-2 of 'The Bear and I' and use vocabulary in context.
lessonSequence.grammar: Descriptive prepositions (by the hole, on the ice).

stages.activity: Listen to Arctic howling wind SFX; imagine sitting on frozen sea ice.
Pre-teach page 42 Words in Context with TPR gestures.
Choral read stanzas 1-2 on page 43; identify rhyming and sensory words.
Draw and label an Arctic fishing hole with the fisherman.
Mime and say: 'The ice is thin!'

lessonSequence.title: The Crack in the Ice: Shared Danger
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to read stanzas 3-4 and explain the ice trap conflict.
targetChunks: made a trap for us both
lessonSequence.grammar: Past simple and present continuous narrative verbs (cracked, walking).

stages.activity: Review stanzas 1-2; mimic heavy bear footsteps.
Read stanzas 3-4; trigger ice-cracking sound on smartboard.
Analyze why the situation is a trap for both man and bear.
Reader's theatre: students read narrator and bear perspective lines.
Answer: 'Why did the ice crack?'

lessonSequence.title: Not Enemies Today: Poetry Recitation & Phonics
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to recite the poem resolution and master final '-ng' words.

stages.activity: Read stanzas 5-6; discuss why the fisherman backed away.
Introduce final '-ng' blend on page 47; contrast thin / thing.
Phonics tongue twister chant; circle -ng words in poem.
Complete page 46 Venn Diagram comparing fisherman and polar bear.
Say two words ending with '-ng'.

lessonSequence.title: The Trouble with Gasoline: City Smog
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to describe how traditional gasoline cars pollute city air.
lessonSequence.grammar: Present simple for scientific facts ('Cars burn gasoline').

stages.activity: Audio comparison: roar of gasoline traffic vs quiet forest.
Teach page 48 vocabulary; read page 49 about crude oil and exhaust smog.
Smartboard activity: wipe smog away to clean the city skyline.
Write 2 problems caused by gasoline cars in notebooks.
Name the fossil fuel that gasoline comes from (crude oil).

lessonSequence.title: Plant Power & Batteries: Biofuel & Electric Cars
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to explain how biofuel and electric cars work and use 'instead of'.
lessonSequence.grammar: Substitution with 'instead of' ('electricity instead of gasoline').

stages.activity: Show corn cob and car battery; ask: 'How can these move a car?'
Read pp.50-51; explain plant biofuel and rechargeable battery technology.
Sentence builder on smartboard using 'instead of'.
Pairs debate: 'Electric cars are better because ___.'
Say one advantage of electric cars (zero smoke).

lessonSequence.title: Sunlight on Wheels: Solar Cars & Comparatives
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to compare vehicles using comparative adjectives.

stages.activity: Examine photo of futuristic solar car racing across sunny highway.
Read pp.52-53; teach comparative adjective rules (-er vs more).
Complete page 54 Car Features Comparison Matrix.
Write 2 comparative sentences comparing electric cars to gas cars.
Oral check: 'Electric cars are ___ than gasoline cars.'

lessonSequence.title: Saving the Arctic Ice: Climate Action Showcase
lessonSequence.objective: Pupils will be able to map environmental cause-and-effect chains and present their action plan.

stages.activity: Choral recitation of key poem and car slogans.
Review page 55 graphic organizer: Clean Cars -> Less Smog -> Thick Ice -> Polar Bears.
Complete Action Plan organizer in pairs.
Pair presentation: 'How clean cars help polar bears survive.'
Add your eco-pledge to the smartboard planet tree.
